#1 I thought I'd briefly introduce myself and explain the perspective from which I'll be asking questions.
(English isn't my first language, so I appreciate your patience if my wording is occasionally awkward.)

I've always been drawn to spatial puzzles. I spent years enjoying Rubik's Cubes (including higher-dimensional variants), and video games like Manifold Garden, Superliminal, Antichamber, Patrick's Parabox, and Baba is You. Looking back, I think all of these interests point toward the same question: is there a way of learning mathematics that begins with meaning and structure, with symbolic formalism introduced as a precise language for ideas that are already understood intuitively?

My educational path has been unconventional, almost entirely a self-directed journey. One difficulty I had with my experience of formal education was that I often encountered procedures before explanations. I found it difficult to stay motivated when I couldn't understand the underlying reasons or conceptual picture. That mismatch eventually led me to leave formal education and continue learning on my own.

Over time I discovered ideas like category theory, functional programming, and dependent type theory. Later I encountered representational formalisms such as string diagrams, geometric algebra, root systems,... and eventually resources such as "Picturing Quantum Processes". They often seem to start from semantics and conceptual structure before symbolic manipulation.

Part of the reason I'm sharing it is that I suspect there are others with similarly unconventional backgrounds who have found themselves asking the same kinds of questions, even if they arrived here by different paths. If someone like that happens to read this, I'd like them to know they're not alone.

My question is whether this "semantics-first" style has an established tradition within more general topics such as abstract formalization, mathematical logic or foundations of physics. Right now, my immediate goal is to learn the language of string diagrams, geometric algebra and to have an intuition about the progression of modalities (from the scratch).
So, an even more concrete question: Is there a text or set of talks that develops the modalities in a diagrammatic, string-diagram-friendly way? (Underneath that, I’m also wondering: Is there a visual way - a genuinely pictorial, spatial, manipulable language - that lets me see the deep structural invariants of logic itself?)

Thanks for reading.
Best,
- Benjamin

(P.S. Thanks to Urs for the pointer. I can see the broad outline for the landscape now, although much of the formalism is still beyond me. I'll be working through the lecture notes "Modern Physics formalized in Modal Homotopy Type Theory; Logical Topology and Axiomatic Cohesion", they look like a promising place to build intuition.)
